2043108284970995805: The optical infrastructure bubble may last longer and more persistently than expected. The market has now begun to accept this technology as essential infrastructure rather than just a trend, and from that moment on, capital is excessively concentrated in one direction. The problem is not whether this trend was wrong, but that it was correct too quickly. It is necessary to recall Cisco's past cases. At that time, Internet traffic was actually growing explosively, and there was also a clear demand for network equipment. The company grew, the industry expanded, and the direction itself was perfectly right. However, the stock price took a different path. The market reflected the future in prices too quickly, and because infrastructure always has the property of being installed ahead of demand, CAPEX was executed excessively. In the end, by the time the performance was confirmed as reality, expectations had already been exhausted, and after that, it was not a matter of growth but a collapse of valuation. The current optical infrastructure closely resembles this trend. Of course, it is difficult to explain a company like NVIDIA using the same frame. This is because they are not simple infrastructure providers but platform operators that hold the center of AI computation and have a structure that simultaneously controls hardware, software, and the ecosystem. But the optics are different. Optics is an essential technology, but at the same time, it has a strong infrastructure nature that exists on a standardized and distributed supply chain. It is an area where substitutability exists, multiple players can enter simultaneously, and technological superiority is unlikely to lead to a long-term monopoly. In particular, the reason why optics is attracting attention now is clear. Because it is a bottleneck. Almost all problems in AI infrastructure, including power efficiency, heat generation, data transmission distance, and signal loss, ultimately arise from interconnect, and the solutions are converging on optics. The market places the expectation that excess profits will continue in the long term for companies that resolve this bottleneck. But historically bottleneck industries always follow the same path. The moment a bottleneck is identified, capital flows in, supply expands, competition intensifies, and margins ultimately compress. What the market is seeing now is ‘demand’, and what the stock price is reflecting is the ‘complete future’. There is always a time difference between these two. Initially, expectations drive up multiples, then CAPEX expands, and at some point, supply begins to outstrip demand. From then on, even if sales increase, the stock price may actually fall. As Cisco did in the past, industry growth continues, but the return on investment follows a completely different trajectory. Another important point is that the optics industry itself is an area where it is structurally difficult to ‘secure first place.’ Technology standards are constantly changing, customers are concentrated in a few hyperscalers, and they are willing to reorganize or internalize their supply chains whenever necessary. In a structure where packaging, materials, and design are separated, it is not easy for a specific company to dominate the entire value chain. Ultimately, the assumption that No. 1 now will also be No. 1 in the future is particularly vulnerable in this industry. In the end, the key is simple. Optical infrastructure is not the wrong direction. Rather, the market is likely to grow much larger in the future. As the structure of data centers changes and AI calculations explode, optics will become a necessity, not an option. However, the problem is the expectation that the fruits of that growth will belong exclusively to a specific company, and that this expectation is already excessively reflected in the current stock price. Good industry and good investment are not the same thing. The industry may be right, but the timing may be wrong. The current optical market stands right on the borderline. Therefore, in this period, it is more important to recognize the gap between expectations and reality than to be sure of the direction.

2040669466674217410: Does it look different when you sit high up? ㅣ260405 1. It is no coincidence that executive offices are always located at the corners of high floors. In large corporations around the world, executives above vice president are almost without exception placed in high-rise corner offices. The place where the view is open in all directions with two or more sides of glass is not simply a large room, but is a spatial expression of the scale of thinking that the organization expects from that person. Where you sit determines how you think. 2. The view from above changes the way humans think. In psychology, research results have repeatedly emerged showing a connection between physical height and the level of abstract thinking. As you go higher, details disappear and the overall structure and flow become visible, and this visual experience naturally increases the unit of thought. It is not unrelated to this principle that people who see the big picture are ultimately able to make big decisions. 3. On the other hand, a low seat with a blocked view constricts your thoughts. Employees working in windowless office spaces tend to have high stress levels, define problems narrowly, and focus only on short-term solutions. A physically blocked space also causes psychologically blocked accidents. If the environment is narrow, your thoughts will also become narrow accordingly. 4. A view is not just a view, but a cognitive resource. In a study by the MIT Graduate School of Architecture, productivity improved by about 23% in an office environment with natural light and external views. It has been confirmed that being able to see the outside itself acts as a kind of restorative stimulus to the brain, maintaining concentration and judgment. In the end, a good view is not an aesthetic element but a functional element directly related to performance. 5. There is a long-standing organizational psychological context behind the high-rise corner office becoming a symbol of power. In American work culture, the corner office has been considered the “most important person’s seat” for decades, and people who occupy that position naturally internalize the perception that they must play a more important role. It is a structure in which space creates role expectations, and those expectations lead to actual behavior and performance. 6. High visibility leads to long-term thinking. In a study by behavioral economist Richard Fisher, the decision quality of people who think from a long-term perspective and those who only react in the short-term vary dramatically over time. The farther you look, the more likely you are to make critical decisions without being swayed by the noise in front of you. This is exactly the same principle as the physical experience of seeing widely from high up. If you go up high, you will see far away, and if you look far away, it will slowly shake. 7. Successful leaders have instinctively practiced this principle. Warren Buffett took a broad view of the entire market despite working in Omaha rather than New York's Wall Street, and Steve Jobs designed the flow of the entire experience before detail, all in the same context. They were not in a specific position, but always maintained the habit of looking furthest from the highest viewpoint. The height of vision determines the height of performance. 8. The same principle works in housing. Studies have repeatedly reported that people living in high-rise residential spaces with secured views have higher psychological stability and self-efficacy than those living in environments without such views. Seeing a wide-open landscape without feeling stuffy every morning has an impact on determining the size of your thoughts for the day. The quality of life and thinking are connected to the quality of what we see. 9. In the end, “where you live is important” is not about real estate. The scale of a person is created by accumulating the perspective with which he or she starts the day, works, and thinks every day. A low, narrow, and closed environment makes thinking low, narrow, and closed, and a high, wide, and open environment has the opposite effect. The environment is a quiet variable that sets the upper limit of thinking. 10. If you cannot sit in a corner office on a high floor right now, the next step is to raise the altitude of your thoughts first. The starting point is to train your perspective to look down on any problem from one level above and intentionally expand the landscape you see. It's not that people who sit high up think differently, but those who practice thinking differently first eventually get there. The view is the starting point, not the destination.
2040756648566989238: It seems like Google has sharpened its sword... 🫨 They have applied for a patent aimed at reducing the memory dependence of the LLM model. [0009] This technique reduces the transmission of model parameters in multiple layers and reduces the transmission of attention cache data in the attention layer, thereby reducing overall processing latency. The system achieves these benefits without having to allocate additional extremely limited on-chip memory to store model weights or attention cache data. These techniques do not require larger on-chip memory (e.g., memory in the processor or accelerator) and do not increase the on-chip memory allocation. [0010] The system can reduce the amount of on-chip memory required or the amount of on-chip memory used. As explained in more detail below, the system can perform the step of predicting the top k weights or tokens using an approximation matrix that has a smaller data size or memory storage size than the full matrix of the neural network. In some implementations, the approximation matrix for each layer of the neural network can be trained or adjusted to predict the top k elements of that layer to a predetermined level of accuracy, often during the neural network training process. Once training is complete, the approximation matrix for the layer can be stored along with the overall weights or parameters and used during inference. The size of the approximation matrix can be made smaller, for example, by storing parameter values ​​for a smaller number of parameters (e.g. using a low-order approximation matrix) or by quantizing the parameter values ​​to reduce the number of bits required for each parameter value. As a result, loading an approximation matrix requires less data to be transferred to the on-chip memory of an accelerator or other processor than transferring the original matrix. Once the weight subset (including the top k weights) is determined, the system can load only a portion of the weights from the original matrix for that layer. Instead of sending the entire matrix, the system can load and process only selected parts of the matrix (for example, load and process only the weights contained in a subset, or load and process only a specific group of weights that contains the weights contained in the subset). Therefore, the maximum on-chip memory capacity required to process a neural network layer can be reduced because the approximation matrix and the selected portion of the full matrix used in a given processing cycle are smaller than the data size of the full matrix.

2040391475478077730: As soon as quantum sensing starts to make money, the biggest obstacle will be how to turn those fragile quantum states into practical machines. Existing quantum systems were packed with lasers, mirrors, and control devices on an optical table. It was large, consumed a lot of power, and had a structure where signals were damaged by vibration or temperature changes. This SWAP (Size, Weight, And Power) bottleneck was the real wall blocking the commercialization of quantum sensing. The solution that Infleqtion focuses on is ‘Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC)’. It is a method of integrating a laser array, miniature frequency comb, and spatial light modulator into one chip using silicon photonics technology. Through this, we aim to reduce size, weight, power, and cost (C-SWaP) by 10 to up to 10,000 times. Just looking at the Tiqker optical atomic clock roadmap, this direction is clear. Starting from the current 3U rack size, it is expected to expand to data centers, AI clusters, and defense and space fields as it undergoes PIC integration and is compressed to ≤3U and even <0.5L. We are already verifying picosecond-level precise timing in the field in White Rabbit integration with Safran, Royal Navy submarine demonstration, and Quantum Corridor network testing. Added to this is ‘AI-based quantum control.’ Like Q-CTRL or Infleqtion's Contextual Machine Learning (CML), the software compensates for noise and suppresses decoherence in real time. It is a strategy to compensate for the physical vulnerabilities of hardware with software. As a result, inertial navigation in GPS-denied environments and ultra-high sensitivity magnetic field and gravity measurements can operate reliably even on actual moving platforms (submarines, drones, vehicles). The strengths of the neutral atom platform shine even brighter here. As sensing (Tiqker, inertial sensor) and computing (Sqale) share the same hardware stack, the PIC miniaturization effect can be applied to both at the same time. Unlike NV centers or other solid-state sensors, rubidium-based neutral atoms are relatively advantageous for precise control even near room temperature, and the possibility of mass production using meta-surfaces is high. Of course, complete chip-scale integration is still in progress. Remaining challenges include manufacturing yield, cost optimization, and long-term stability in extreme environments (vibration and magnetic fields). However, looking at Infleqtion's financial update for 2025-2026 and demonstrations from CES 2026, there are strong signs that these technology variables are quickly becoming a reality. In the end, the real game changer in quantum sensing is not “how to turn the weaknesses of the quantum state into strengths,” but how quickly the combination of PIC miniaturization + AI control reaches the level of practical deployment. The most exciting point right now is that Infleqtion is pushing both axes simultaneously with its neutral atom single platform.

2038866062507155815: - The story behind TurboQuant. For reference, if you look at the papers cited by TurboQuant, there is one paper written by Koreans. Reference[59] in the TurboQuant paper And I will share what was said in this paper and by field gurus. (I have also posted a few posts related to this since last year. Last year, a major memory researcher in China was KV Cache...) ———- 1. KV cache compression is not an issue that came out of nowhere, but a growing trend that has already been building up. The recent debate surrounding the memory industry seems to have changed the game with the emergence of a certain technology, but in reality, that is not the case. Methods for reducing or handling KV cache have been studied for a long time, and there is not just one method. Attempts have continued to reduce the computational burden by expressing data with fewer bits, removing less important parts, grouping similar information, or changing the structure itself. What has changed recently is that there is a shift from the attitude of “let’s keep the original version as much as possible” to “it is okay to reduce it more drastically as long as the core meaning is maintained.” As agent-type AI increases, it is no longer simply a matter of reducing a chunk of cache, but an important issue is how to handle the entire task state and context that comes and goes in the intermediate inference stage more lightly and efficiently. In other words, rather than an improvement in storage technology, it is more correct to view it as a trend that changes the way AI carries on thinking itself to be more efficient. 2. Even if compression technology develops, memory demand is likely to increase rather than decrease. On the surface, compressing the cache appears to reduce memory use. But real markets don't work that simple. As costs go down, companies and services will not only do existing tasks more cheaply, but will also try longer context processing, more complex question and answering, more concurrent users, and more agent integrations that were previously considered too burdensome. This is similar to the phenomenon that widening the road does not make car movement easier, but rather causes more cars to gather. The same goes for AI services now. Features such as long-winded reasoning, multiple consecutive conversations, multi-agent operations, and maintaining session state still require a lot of memory. Therefore, efficiency technology is closer to a technology that opens up uses that have been closed due to cost, rather than a technology that eliminates memory demand. In the end, the key is not how much less memory is used on a single server, but how much larger the overall service scale and inference volume can be. 3. The real problem is not the importance of memory, but that memory companies are still lagging behind. Memory is still a very important component of AI infrastructure. However, the fact that it is an important component and the fact that it is leading the market are different. In fact, much of the high added value is already moving to higher-level areas such as computational chips such as GPUs and NPUs, packaging, interconnects, controllers, and system software. HBM is also an example of this trend. Memory itself is essential, but money and influence are generated not from individual memories, but from how they are tied to the entire system. However, the memory industry is still accustomed to large-scale facility investments, long development cycles, and standards-centered thinking. Simply put, the method is, “When the market grows sufficiently and the requirements become clear, we will supply accordingly.” The problem is that the AI ​​market does not wait that long. Service companies or model developers are busy running and optimizing models within a given hardware environment, and do not design new memory structures on their behalf. Therefore, in the future, memory companies should more actively explain which memory structures are advantageous for which AI tasks, what speed and capacity configurations are necessary, and why such structures are meaningful in the market. 2038782950599524388: The biggest reason why the memory semiconductor fab operates at 100% is due to process characteristics. Therefore, to be more precise, rather than continuing to operate due to fixed costs, the best option is to operate at 100% because the fixed costs are inevitably high due to the special nature of the semiconductor process. To produce memory, hundreds of steps, including major processes such as exposure, etching, and deposition, must be continuously interconnected. In this situation, if the line is stopped even for a moment, the entire process must be inspected when restarted, so it takes several months to reestablish the yield, and if the clean room environment is reset, time and cost increase explosively. In addition, since certain equipment must maintain high temperature/high vacuum conditions at all times, turning it off even for a short period of time can cause greater damage, both from the yield point of view as mentioned above. In other words, it is difficult to physically stop the process due to the nature of the process. Even if some factories stop or reduce production, fixed costs such as depreciation, labor, and clean room maintenance remain the same, so even if you are losing money due to memory prices, continuing production without stopping will inevitably reduce losses even a little compared to not producing. Due to the nature of the process, the burden of fixed costs increases, which is why the factory must continue to operate even if it is at a deficit. That is why memory companies such as Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron are considering expansion. Demand appears to be good, so once capacity is expanded, production cannot be reduced. In this way, if demand forecasting fails, excess inventory becomes a factor, and excess inventory becomes a factor in reducing memory prices. Because of these factors, memory semiconductors are classified as commodities.

2038209644120666452: Formfactor company appears in this article, but since it is only a brief technical explanation, I will write about FormFactor company's Pharos Probe Series in more detail. The Pharos Probe Series (especially the Pharos Edge Short Lens / Long Lens versions) is an optical probe developed to directly test silicon photonics (SiPh) chips in the wafer state. This is a technology that allows the entire wafer to be inspected without the need to dice the chips and make them into individual dies as in the existing method. The key is an ultra-precision 3D-printed micro-lens (Pharos lens) made with 'two-photon lithography'. This lens adopts a periscope structure to efficiently bend the vertical light coming down from the optical fiber 90 degrees horizontally and accurately inject (couple) it into the edge (side) waveguide of the chip. <1. ‘Nano-precision 3D printing’ technology made with two-photon lithography> This technology is on a different level from regular 3D printers. Think of it as ultra-precision micro-sculpture, where a laser pen is used to “draw” point by point into liquid resin and harden it. Because the laser hardens the resin only by absorbing two photons simultaneously, the reaction occurs only in an extremely small volume (nanometer level) that is in focus. So you can freely create 3D shapes in air or liquid. While traditional lenses are made by glass grinding or injection molding, Pharos lenses 3D print complex freeform optical structures in one step at nanometer resolution. Result: Even though it is ultra-small (micrometer size), optical loss is extremely low, and the custom Mode Field Diameter (MFD, the size at which light spreads) can be precisely matched to the waveguide. Light efficiency is maximized, as if “fitting the pipe diameter to prevent water leakage.” This makes the lens extremely small, light and precise, allowing it to easily fit into narrow trenches or V-grooves on the wafer. <2. Periscope structure — the magic of ‘smartly’ bending vertical light horizontally> Optical fibers usually send light vertically down from above. However, the waveguide of a silicon photonics chip is located on the side (edge) of the chip, so light must be input horizontally to work properly. It's just like a submarine periscope! The submarine is hidden underwater, but we use the periscope mirror to ‘see’ the ocean above horizontally, then turn 90 degrees to look inside the submarine. The Pharos lens also uses 3D printing to create a periscope structure, such as a micro-mirror or prism, inside the lens, which bends vertically incident light exactly 90 degrees to create a horizontal beam and shoots it to the edge of the chip. Thanks to this structure, the coupling loss is very low at less than 1.5 dB (maximum 1.51 dB/facet) and there is almost no polarization dependence. Existing tapered lensed fibers had to be aligned manually, and they were difficult to use in production because they easily damaged chips or had large alignment errors. Pharos lenses feature self-alignment + patented fiducial (optical reference points) that enable automatic calibration at the nanometer level. <3. Pharos Edge Short Lens vs Long Lens — ‘Customized’ version optimized for V-groove / Trench > Silicon wafers are pre-etched with a trench (rectangular groove) or V-groove (V-shaped groove) for edge coupling. Short Lens: Optimized for shorter trench depth and short working distance. Quickly tests by fitting into a narrow, shallow groove. Long Lens: Optimized for deeper V-groove and long working distance. The V-shaped groove is deep, so the lens is designed to be long so that light can be accurately injected from a greater distance. Additional Vertical version: for grating coupler (surface grating coupler), also supports vertical coupling. Just as the vehicle type (short/long lens) is selected depending on whether the car parking lot entrance is narrow, straight (trench) or slanted, V-shaped (V-groove), the optimal lens is selected according to the shape and depth of the groove to achieve the highest efficiency. <4. So why is this technology innovative? > (1) Wafer-level full automated testing Thousands of measurements can be made on one wafer. The existing lab method took several days to several months due to manual + dicing post-testing, but Pharos is capable of testing within 5 seconds per die, repeatability within 0.2 dB, and long-term stability at the level of 0.01 dB. (2) Productivity explosion SiPh chips such as data centers, AI accelerators, LiDAR, 5G optical transceivers, and quantum optical devices can be tested immediately at the mass production stage, greatly shortening the time-to-yield. (3) Full integration with FormFactor system interconnection CM300xi-SiPh probe station + Velox software + AutoCal (automatic calibration). It is designed so that even beginners can use it easily.

2037809751644643665: In some ways, TurboQuant is a panic cell behind the development of good technology, which led to a plunge in memory prices. Do you really feel that memory demand will decrease? You can first solve the genius quiz that I posted as a comment in another post, and then come back to this post. It seems more appropriate to view KV cache, which is mentioned as a major application of TurboQuant, not as "external long-term storage memory" (GPU memory itself, such as HBM or DDR), but as "working memory" that is maintained in real time during inference (running time). As a temporary cache memory that continues to store the Key and Value of previous tokens when the model processes conversations or long contexts. Why is this important? Previously, as the context length became longer, the KV cache consumed GPU memory exponentially. (sometimes up to 80-90% of inference memory) TurboQuant compresses this KV cache by ~6x (3-bit level) without loss of accuracy, while speeding up attention operations by up to 8x. (Based on H100) As a result, what can be done with the same hardware increases significantly as follows: 1. Context length significantly increases → Contexts that are 4 to 6 times (or more) longer can be processed with the same memory. Significant improvements in long document summaries, codebase-wide analysis, very long multi-turn conversations, and Agentic AI, where agents remember multiple steps. 2. Increased concurrent user/batch size → More requests can be processed simultaneously with the same server → Service capacity increased by nearly 6 times (since memory bottleneck is resolved). 3. Cost efficiency → You can do more with the same GPU or achieve similar performance with a cheaper GPU. Did you answer the quiz attached to the image? I believe that answer number 2 (“Fill all 6 slots and receive 6 times more services/subscribers”) is a much more realistic and aggressive strategy. Like number 1, “buy only one memory and save money” is only a short-term cost saving, but is likely to be a missed opportunity in the long run, and is also not a correct understanding when looking at the actual location of the KV cache. These efficiency gains (similar to the Jevons paradox) may appear to reduce memory demand in the short term, but in the long term, as AI services become cheaper and more powerful, they are likely to explode overall demand (longer contexts, more usage). The same article came out saying that memory usage would be reduced to 1/6, but I shouted “a big hit” and the market shouted “a crash.” If it develops in a healthy direction, we expect that it will be an opportunity for expansion of AI base and increase in memory demand, rather than a decrease in memory demand.

2034996675295809984: Photonics Supercycleㅣ260320 1. As of 2026, silicon photonics and CPO (Co-Packaged Optics) have completely moved beyond the stage of simple new technologies and have become the actual core foundation of AI data center infrastructure. At a time when AI clusters require node bandwidths of more than 100Tb/s, the existing copper-based electrical signaling method has reached physical limitations, and only light-based transmission methods can fundamentally solve this bottleneck. 2. The key trigger for this transition is the “Copper Wall”. Because high-speed electrical signals begin to deteriorate when transmitted more than about 1 meter, AI clusters were confined to single racks or small rows. On the other hand, silicon photonics can transmit over 100 meters without signal loss, making it a reality to bundle an AI factory with a scale of 'one million GPUs' into one logical resource. 3. CPO is a structure that drastically shortens the electrical path by integrating the switch ASIC and optical engine in the same package. This relaxes signal equalization requirements and simultaneously reduces power consumption and latency. It has an overwhelming advantage in both energy efficiency and bandwidth compared to the traditional pluggable optical module method. 4. TSMC's COUPE (Compact Universal Photonic Engine) platform is currently in the final mass production verification stage and is scheduled for full-scale mass production in the second half of 2026. Both NVIDIA and Broadcom are building their own CPO solutions based on this platform and SoIC-X 3D packaging technology. Submillimeter-level interconnect distances are realized by stacking 65nm optical integrated circuits (PICs) directly on electronic ICs. 5. NVIDIA and Broadcom have different strategic directions. NVIDIA is combining NVLink and CPO to build a vertically integrated performance fortress within its AI ecosystem, while Broadcom is taking a strategy to leverage its existing installed base by spreading CPO as an open industry standard across Ethernet networks. The competition between the two giants is structured to further speed up the entire CPO ecosystem. 6. STMicroelectronics officially began mass production of silicon photonics for AI data centers in March 2026 and announced plans to more than quadruple production by 2027. Tower Semiconductor has officially confirmed its plan to triple its SiPh production capacity by mid-2026. This is not just a development phase, but a physical investment based on long-term capacity reservations from actual hyperscaler customers. 7. Technology trends in the silicon photonics market in 2026 are largely summarized into four categories. The first is the advancement of optical module speed from 1.6T to 3.2T, the second is heterogeneous integration of SiPh + TFLN (thin film lithium niobate) / III-V platform, the third is the expansion of optical interconnects to replace copper inside AI systems, and the fourth is the emergence of the 'optical chiplet' marketplace through UCIe-S/UCIe-A standardization. 8. From a supply chain perspective, the benefits of this flow are distributed throughout the broader value chain. Starting from substrate materials ($AX T I's indium substrate, $IQ E's compound semiconductor epiwafer), the ecosystem extends to optical transceiver manufacturing ($AAO I, $LIT E, $COH R), test and measurement ($KEY S, $VIA V, $FOR M), optical fiber infrastructure ($GL W, Fujikura, Sumitomo), and foundry and packaging ($TS M, $TSE M, $UM C).
